passage:
In the hostel sick room, Urmila lay under a thin blanket with a fever while her phone kept buzzing. Darshan, a senior from her department, had forwarded the same message four times: "Herbal kadha CURED my cousin's fever the very next morning. Doctors won't tell you this." Then a photo of a steaming cup. Then: "Have you tried it yet??"
Urmila felt pressured and a bit guilty, as if not trying it meant she didn't want to get better. Her roommate brought a cup from the mess anyway, and she sipped it because it was warm.
The campus doctor, checking on her that evening, glanced at the screen. "Fevers like this usually settle with rest, whatever people drink," she said. "Tell me if it keeps going or you feel worse."
Two days later, fever gone, Darshan wrote: "See? The kadha worked!" Urmila typed a reply, deleted it, and sent a thumbs-up.

qa.q: What did Darshan's forwarded message claim?
qa.a: That herbal kadha cured a cousin's fever the very next morning.

qa.q: How did the repeated messages make Urmila feel?
qa.a: Pressured and a bit guilty, as if not trying the kadha meant she didn't want to get better.

qa.q: What could Urmila say back to Darshan without starting a fight?
qa.a: She could thank Darshan for caring and say the doctor told her fevers like hers usually settle with rest, so nobody can tell what the kadha did.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Urmila's recovery?
qa.a: As proof the kadha worked, because she got better after drinking it, without considering that the fever would likely have gone anyway.

grounding: It shows a student on the receiving end of forwarded cure claims whose timing sounds convincing but ignores natural recovery.

passage:
Dear Vijay Mama,
Thank you for all the messages this week. I know you send them because you worry about Mummy's back. The one about the leaf paste says a man in Salem was walking normally two days after using it, and the video looks so real.
But I've been thinking. Mummy's back pain also eases by itself sometimes, after rest, and then comes back. If she had tried the paste in a good week, we'd have thanked the paste. And the man in Salem, we don't know what else he did, or whether he saw a doctor too.
This is hard for me, because I don't want to sound rude to you, and part of me wants the paste to work. Mummy is seeing her doctor on Friday, and I'll ask about it there.
With love,
Preeti

qa.q: What does the message about the leaf paste claim?
qa.a: That a man in Salem was walking normally two days after using it.

qa.q: Why does Preeti feel this letter is hard to write?
qa.a: Preeti doesn't want to sound rude to Mama, and part of Preeti wants the paste to work, so doubting it feels uncomfortable.

qa.q: What is sensible about Preeti's plan?
qa.a: Taking the question to Mummy's doctor on Friday puts the decision with someone who knows her back, instead of trusting a video.

qa.q: How might Vijay Mama feel reading this letter?
qa.a: He might feel a little corrected but also loved, since Preeti starts by thanking him and says the messages come from worry. 🤍

grounding: It shows a student receiving forwarded cure stories whose timing sounds convincing while ignoring natural ups and downs and other causes.

passage: Santosh, remember that rash on my arms in first year? Here's Lalit's official confession about it. Within a day, the family group was full of forwards. Chitti sent one about a neem and turmeric paste: "Boy in Madurai, skin clear in one week!" Then Periappa sent the same thing with a before-and-after photo. Then three more relatives. Every morning I woke up to "Did you try it?" I felt like if I didn't, I was insulting everyone who cared. So I tried it, and I also went to the college clinic because it itched like crazy. The doctor said it was probably a reaction to the new detergent. I switched soap, kept using the paste, and it cleared. Chitti still says it was the paste. Honestly? I can't tell. Nobody can, from that.

qa.q: What did the college clinic doctor say caused the rash?
qa.a: Probably a reaction to the new detergent.

qa.q: How did the flood of forwards make Lalit feel?
qa.a: Lalit felt that not trying the paste would insult everyone who cared, so the messages felt more like pressure than help.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that was wise, and what made the result unclear?
qa.a: Going to the clinic and switching soap was sensible, but using the paste at the same time means nobody can tell what cleared the rash.

qa.q: Why does Chitti keep believing it was the paste?
qa.a: The rash cleared after the paste was used, and Chitti had sent the tip out of care, so seeing it 'work' feels like proof.

grounding: It shows a student receiving viral cure forwards whose before-and-after timing ignores other causes like the change of soap.

passage:
I'm Vishal, and I share a desk with Usha in our second-year chemistry lab. Last week she came in with her voice almost gone and a scarf round her neck.
By the first break her phone had buzzed maybe fifteen times. She showed me one message from her aunt: "Tulsi-ginger leaf water CURED a boy in two days! Doctors don't want you to know." Another from a family group had a photo of a smiling man and "Took it at night, fine by morning."
Usha kept reading them and then putting the phone face down. She said, "Everyone's so sure. What if I don't try it and it gets worse?" She looked tired and a bit cornered.
On Thursday she went to the campus clinic anyway. By Monday her voice was back. The aunt sent another message: "See? The leaf water!" Usha hadn't drunk it.

qa.q: What did the aunt's message say the leaf water did?
qa.a: It said tulsi-ginger leaf water "CURED a boy in two days".

qa.q: What was Usha worried about as the messages kept coming?
qa.a: She was worried that ignoring such confident messages might make her throat worse, and she seemed tired and a bit cornered by all the pressure.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Usha, and what does the ending show about the forwards?
qa.a: Going to the campus clinic worked; the aunt crediting leaf water Usha never drank shows how timing alone can make a cure story sound true.

qa.q: What is it like for Usha to receive so many forwards while she is unwell?
qa.a: It adds pressure and guilt when Usha just wants to rest, because each confident message makes her feel she is doing something wrong by not trying it.

grounding: It shows a student receiving forwards claiming a herb cured someone right after taking it, while timing ignores natural recovery and other causes.

passage:
Monday: Kamal, twenty, limped home from football with a sore knee. By night his Rukmini Chachi had sent three voice notes and a forward: "Warm herbal oil, one night, boy in Madurai walked perfectly next day!"
Wednesday: The knee felt better. Kamal had rested, skipped practice and kept it up on a pillow. He'd also rubbed on the oil once, to keep Chachi happy. Chachi sent a thumbs-up and "Told you, the oil!" Kamal almost believed it. Then he thought: which part had worked, the rest or the oil? The Madurai boy's story said nothing about rest.
Saturday: A physiotherapist at the sports centre checked the knee, said it was a mild strain healing on its own, and gave him exercises. Kamal texted Chachi: "Thank you for caring. The physio says rest did most of it." Chachi replied with a single flower.

qa.q: What did the forward say about the boy in Madurai?
qa.a: It said the boy "walked perfectly next day" after one night of warm herbal oil.

qa.q: What made Kamal almost believe the oil had worked, and what made him doubt it?
qa.a: The knee felt better soon after the oil, so the timing was convincing; then he remembered he had also rested, skipped practice and kept it up, and wondered which one had helped.

qa.q: Which choice was the turning point for Kamal?
qa.a: Seeing the physiotherapist, who explained the strain was healing on its own and gave him exercises, instead of crediting the oil because of timing.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Chachi feel when she reads Kamal's reply?
qa.a: Chachi may feel a little deflated that the oil wasn't the answer, but also touched that Kamal thanked her for caring, as her flower suggests.

grounding: It shows a student receiving a forward that claims an oil cured someone right after use, while the timing hides natural recovery and rest.

passage: You want the story, Ujjwal? Fine. I'm Yash, and last winter I had a cough that wouldn't quit. My aunt heard and started forwarding messages. One said a neighbour's son drank some bitter herb water and was cured the very next morning. Another was a video of a man saying his cough vanished after two days of a leaf paste. Every morning, three or four new forwards: "Try this, beta, it WORKED." Honestly, I was tempted. The timing sounded so neat: drink it, wake up fine. But I kept thinking, how many people drank it and stayed sick? Nobody forwards those. And coughs often ease on their own. So I went to the campus clinic instead. The doctor listened to my chest and checked me properly. I got better. My aunt still thinks it was the leaf paste I never took.

qa.q: Who forwarded the cure messages to Yash?
qa.a: Yash's aunt forwarded the messages.

qa.q: Why did Yash feel tempted by the forwards?
qa.a: Yash felt worn down by the cough and tempted, because the stories had such neat timing, drink it and wake up fine, that the herb seemed to work.

qa.q: What choice did Yash make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Yash went to the campus clinic, where a doctor checked properly, instead of trusting stories that never mention the people who stayed sick.

qa.q: How does the aunt probably see Yash's recovery?
qa.a: The aunt probably feels caring and still sure the remedies work, even crediting a leaf paste Yash never took.

grounding: Shows a student receiving forwarded cure stories whose neat timing is tempting, while noticing natural recovery and going to a doctor.

passage:
Tuesday. Lavanya twisted her ankle in the inter-hostel football match. At the college clinic, the doctor strapped it, told her to rest it, and booked her in for physiotherapy.
Friday. The hostel group pinged all evening. A forward claimed a girl in Mysuru rubbed a special herbal oil on a sprain and walked the very next day. Ganga, her roommate, bought a bottle from the market and set it on Lavanya's desk. "Just try it. It worked for that girl overnight." Lavanya rubbed a little on, mostly to make Ganga happy, and felt the pull of the story anyway.
The following Thursday. The ankle was much better. "The oil!" Ganga cried. Lavanya looked at the calendar. She had rested it and done the physio exercises every day. "Or it was just healing, Ganga. That's what the physio said would happen." She kept up the physio and left the oil on the shelf.

qa.q: Where did Lavanya twist her ankle?
qa.a: She twisted it in the inter-hostel football match.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling on Friday when the oil appeared?
qa.a: Lavanya felt the pull of the story and wanted to make Ganga happy, while still unsure the oil did anything.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do on Thursday that showed good thinking?
qa.a: She checked the calendar, remembered the rest and the daily physio exercises, and kept following the physio instead of crediting the oil.

qa.q: How does Ganga see the ankle getting better?
qa.a: Ganga, who clearly cares about Lavanya, sees the recovery as proof the oil worked, because it came after the oil.

grounding: Shows a student receiving a forwarded overnight-cure story and a push to try an oil, then noticing the ankle was healing with rest and physio.

passage: Jasleen, you keep showing me these forwards about miracle leaves, so let your Jaya bua tell you something. When I was twenty, at college in Amritsar, I had a fever that went on and on. There were no phones then, but news still travelled: every neighbour at our door had a story. "Mrs Gill's nephew took this root powder and was up the next morning!" My mother, frightened, wanted to try every one. I wanted to believe too; the stories were so neat. But my professor had once said something I never forgot: "You only hear about the ones who got up the next morning." So I asked Mother to take me back to Dr Bhatia, who ran proper tests and treated me. I took one spoon of the powder, only to please Mother. It took time, but I recovered. Those neighbours still say it was the root powder.

qa.q: What did the neighbours say Mrs Gill's nephew took?
qa.a: Mrs Gill's nephew took a root powder and was up the next morning.

qa.q: Why did the neighbours' stories tempt young Jaya?
qa.a: Jaya was ill, tired and hopeful, and the stories were so neat, taken today and well tomorrow, that the timing felt like proof.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jaya's story?
qa.a: Remembering the professor's words that you only hear about the ones who got up the next morning, and asking Mother to go back to Dr Bhatia for proper tests and treatment.

qa.q: How did Jaya's mother experience the neighbours' stories?
qa.a: Her mother was frightened and wanted to try every remedy, because each story offered hope for her sick daughter.

grounding: Shows a young woman receiving story after story of overnight cures and choosing a doctor over timing that ignored natural recovery.

passage: Afreen's mother had been running a fever for three days, and Afreen had her semester exam the next morning. Her phone would not stop buzzing. The family group was full of forwards: "My neighbour's cousin had the same fever. He drank tulsi-giloy water at night, and by morning it was gone! Share with everyone!" Another message had a photo of a smiling man and the words "Cured in one day." Afreen, exhausted, almost went to the market to buy the herbs. Then her friend Tenzin called. "Afreen, did anyone in those messages say what would have happened without the herb?" "No." "Fevers often go down on their own. The drink just came before." Afreen looked at her mother, pale on the bed. That evening she took her to the clinic, and the doctor ran tests. Afreen studied in the waiting room.

qa.q: How many days had Afreen's mother had a fever?
qa.a: For three days.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as the forwards kept coming?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and tempted, pulled toward the herbal cure because the story said the fever went right after.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's question help Afreen see, and what did she do?
qa.a: That the messages never showed what would have happened without the herb; she took her mother to the clinic for tests that evening.

qa.q: How might the people sharing the forwards see their messages?
qa.a: They probably believe they are helping, not noticing that the story only shows one fever ending after one drink.

grounding: Shows a student receiving forwards claiming a herb cured a fever right after taking it, until a friend points out natural recovery and a doctor is seen.

passage: In the Delhi hostel, Kashish's phone lit up again. It was a forward from her aunt: a video of a man saying he had taken a spoon of a special seed powder every morning and his joint pain disappeared in a week. "Share with all your elders!" the caption said. Kashish almost forwarded it to her father, whose knee had been hurting. Then she remembered her statistics class. Her roommate Payal, a pharmacy student, looked at the video. "He took the powder, and then he felt better. Does he say whether it was going to get better anyway? Or what else he changed?" Kashish watched again. The man mentioned, in passing, that he'd also started walking every day and had seen a physiotherapist. "So it could be the walking, or time," Kashish said. She didn't forward it. Instead she called her father and asked if he'd seen his doctor about the knee.

qa.q: What did the man in the video take every morning?
qa.a: A spoon of a special seed powder.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she first saw the video?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and worried, tempted to forward it because her father's knee had been hurting.

qa.q: What did Kashish do instead of forwarding the video?
qa.a: She called her father and asked if he had seen his doctor about the knee.

qa.q: How does Payal see the man's story?
qa.a: Payal sees it as timing, not proof, since he never says whether the pain would have eased anyway or what else he changed.

grounding: Shows a student receiving a forward claiming a powder cured pain right after taking it, and noticing other causes and natural recovery before sharing.

passage:
Last winter my father had a bad cough that wouldn't go, and within a day the family group was full of cures. I'm Vidya, the only one in the house studying science, so everyone forwarded everything to me.
One message said a man drank a leaf-and-honey paste and "the next morning, cough gone!" Another was a video of a woman crying with joy after taking a herbal powder. The timing made them sound so convincing: took it, then recovered.
But I kept thinking: how many people took the paste and didn't get better? They don't make videos. And lots of coughs get better on their own. The paste just happened to be there when that happened.
Still, it was exhausting to be the one saying "wait". I felt like the family villain.
In the end Karthik, my cousin who's a nurse, backed me, and Papa went to the doctor that evening.

qa.q: What did one message say a man drank?
qa.a: One message said a man drank a leaf-and-honey paste and his cough was gone the next morning.

qa.q: What did Vidya feel as the forwards kept coming?
qa.a: Vidya felt exhausted and like the family villain for asking everyone to wait, even while doubting the cures.

qa.q: What helped the family make a safer choice?
qa.a: Karthik, a nurse, backing Vidya, and Papa going to the doctor that evening instead of relying on forwarded cures.

qa.q: How might the relatives sending the videos see Vidya's doubts?
qa.a: They probably felt they were helping out of love, and may have found Vidya's 'wait' cold or stubborn.

grounding: Shows a student receiving forwarded cure stories whose timing sounds convincing while ignoring natural recovery and other causes.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellness room. Written by Sumit, student counsellor.
Kunal, second year, came in looking tired. His phone had forty unread forwards from his family group, most about his father's knee pain. One said an uncle's neighbour rubbed on a herbal oil and "walked normally the next day". Another promised a powder that "fixed joint pain in one week".
Kunal said, "The timing sounds so real. He used it, then he was fine. How can I argue with that?" He felt guilty for doubting, and guilty for not sending money for the oil.
I didn't give any medical view; I'm not a doctor. I asked what else might explain someone feeling better the next day. He listed rest, pain that comes and goes, and other medicine.
What I did next: we drafted a kind message to his family suggesting his father see the doctor first and ask about any oil there. He sent it before leaving.

qa.q: How many unread forwards did Kunal have?
qa.a: Kunal's phone had forty unread forwards from his family group.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling about the forwards?
qa.a: Kunal felt torn and guilty, both for doubting the cures and for not sending money for the oil.

qa.q: Why was the drafted message a good step?
qa.a: It kindly moved the family toward a doctor for the father's knee pain, while leaving room to ask about the oil there.

qa.q: How did Sumit see Kunal during the session?
qa.a: Sumit saw a tired, torn student and chose to ask questions and help with the message rather than give a medical view.

grounding: Shows a student burdened by forwarded cure stories whose timing sounds convincing, seen through a counsellor's note.

passage:
Friday, hostel room 214.
Anirban keeps sending me the same video. A guy with perfect hair says he drank warm lemon water every morning and his headaches "vanished in three days". Anirban means well. He's watched me hold my head through lectures all week.
So I tried it. Day one, headache. Day two, a bit better. Day three, gone. For a moment I thought: it works!
Then I remembered day three was the day after exams ended, the first night I'd slept properly in two weeks. And I'd stopped living on tea. Any of those could have done it. Or the headache just went, the way headaches sometimes do.
I still drink the lemon water; it's nice. But if the headaches come back, I'm going to the health centre, not the video.
Manoj

qa.q: How long did the man in the video say it took for his headaches to vanish?
qa.a: The man said his headaches vanished in three days.

qa.q: Why did Manoj briefly believe the lemon water worked?
qa.a: Manoj felt relieved and hopeful when the headache went on day three, right after starting the lemon water, so the timing felt convincing.

qa.q: What does Manoj plan if the headaches come back, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Manoj plans to go to the health centre, since a doctor can look at the real cause instead of a video.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel if the headaches came back despite the lemon water?
qa.a: Anirban might feel disappointed and a bit worried, having sent the video out of care.

grounding: Shows a student receiving a viral cure video whose timing seems convincing, then remembering sleep, exams and natural recovery.
